lead.t: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) is the most common parasitic infection worldwide, especially among children.

sets.t: Enterobius vermicularis and Ascaris lumbricoides — Essay Questions

snip.t: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) is the most common parasitic infection worldwide, especially among children.
Transmission: Likely fecal-oral, possibly through eggs of *Enterobius vermicularis*.

qs.q: Which anatomical region serves as the primary habitat for adult Enterobius vermicularis worms?
o: Terminal ileum and rectum near the distal colon
Caecum, appendix, and ascending colon of the large intestine
Stomach and pyloric antrum of the upper gastrointestinal tract
Duodenum and proximal jejunum of the small intestine
qs.e: Adult pinworms reside in the caecum, appendix, and ascending colon. The duodenum is instead the hatching site for ingested eggs.

qs.q: Which clinical manifestation is uniquely associated with female genitourinary involvement in heavy Enterobius vermicularis infections?
o: Bilateral hydronephrosis and acute renal failure
qs.e: Female worms can aberrantly migrate into the vulva and vagina, causing vulvovaginitis and mucoid discharge. Painful vesicular lesions are typically viral in origin rather than parasitic.

qs.q: What defines the unique phenomenon of retroinfection in the life cycle of Enterobius vermicularis?
o: Ingested eggs bypass the intestine and hatch inside the bloodstream
Male worms re-enter the appendix after mating
Adult worms travel backward from the rectum into the stomach
Larvae hatch on perianal skin and migrate back into the colon
qs.e: Retroinfection occurs when eggs hatch directly on the perianal skin, and the resulting larvae migrate back through the anus into the colon. Autoinfection, by contrast, involves hand-to-mouth transfer after scratching.

qs.q: Which specific bodily location serves as the primary habitat for adult Enterobius vermicularis worms?
qs.e: Adult pinworms inhabit the cecum, appendix, and adjacent portions of the ascending colon. They do not primarily reside in the upper small intestine like Ascaris.

qs.q: An 8-year-old child with perianal itching is evaluated for a pinworm infection. What is the primary infective form of Enterobius vermicularis ingested during transmission?
qs.e: Transmission occurs via the ingestion of embryonated eggs containing larvae through contaminated fingers, fomites, or food. Unfertilized eggs are not the infective stage.

qs.q: Which mechanism describes how Enterobius vermicularis can maintain a persistent infection without new external exposure?
qs.e: Retroinfection occurs when eggs hatch on the perianal skin, and larvae migrate back into the colon. This is unique to pinworms and contributes to high persistence.

qs.q: A physician suspects Enterobius vermicularis in a school-aged child but orders a perianal tape test instead of a stool ova and parasite exam. Why are standard fecal smears generally ineffective?
qs.e: Eggs are rarely found in feces because gravid females migrate to the perianal region at night to deposit them. Perianal swabs are therefore required for diagnosis.

qs.q: A 7-year-old child is diagnosed with Enterobius vermicularis, and the pediatrician advises treating all household members simultaneously. What is the main reason for this strategy?
qs.e: High recurrence rates due to autoinfection mean that treatment should include all household members to completely clear the infection source. Sharing utensils is not the primary transmission mode.

ai.clinicalScope: Enterobius vermicularis infection (enterobiasis) in children and adolescents presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
ai.title: Enterobius vermicularis Infection
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Pinworm infection is the commonest intestinal helminthiasis worldwide, especially in school‑aged children. It spreads by fecal‑oral transmission of eggs and causes perianal itching, irritability and secondary sleep disturbance.

sections.p: Enterobius vermicularis is a small, white nematode that lives in the human colon and rectum. Adult females migrate nocturnally to the perianal skin to lay thousands of eggs, which cause the classic pruritus.
b: Most prevalent helminth in children; prevalence up to 30 % in some East African schools
Transmission is fecal‑oral; eggs survive on fomites for 2–3 weeks
Outbreaks occur in crowded settings – schools, orphanages, refugee camps

sections.p: A female pinworm measures 8–13 mm; the male is half that size. Eggs are ovoid, 50‑60 µm, with a characteristic flattened side that adheres to skin and fabrics.
b: Life cycle completed in 4‑6 weeks
No intermediate host – direct human‑to‑human spread
Eggs become infective within 4‑6 h after being laid

sections.p: Ingestion of embryonated eggs leads to hatching in the duodenum; larvae mature in the colon. Female worms exit the anus at night to deposit eggs on perianal skin, which are then transferred by scratching or contaminated objects.
b: Key risk behaviours: nail‑biting, thumb‑sucking, sharing bedding
Autoinfection common; reinfection from household members frequent
Eggs resist drying, allowing survival on clothing, toys, toilet seats

sections.p: Enterobiasis is usually mild but can cause significant discomfort and secondary complications, especially in malnourished or immunocompromised children.
b: Perianal pruritus, worse at night – hallmark symptom
Secondary bacterial infection of scratched skin
Rare complications: vulvovaginitis, urinary tract infection, appendicitis‑like pain
Behavioural impact: irritability, sleep loss, reduced school performance

sections.p: Diagnosis relies on detecting characteristic eggs on perianal swab (Scotch‑tape test) performed in the early morning before washing.
b: If tape test unavailable, treat empirically in a typical clinical picture
Repeat tape test on three consecutive mornings to increase sensitivity

t.b: Does the patient have pinworm eggs? Positive microscopy confirms infection; negative does not rule out if sampling is poor
Are eggs present in stool? Low sensitivity; useful when tape test unavailable
Is the clinical picture compatible? Guides need for empirical treatment when tests are absent

sections.p: Single‑dose oral albendazole or mebendazole eradicates adult worms; a second dose 2 weeks later eliminates newly hatched larvae. Environmental hygiene prevents reinfection.
b: Repeat dose after 2 weeks to cover the life cycle
Treat all household contacts simultaneously to break transmission
Wash bedding, underwear, and nightclothes in hot water; clean surfaces with bleach
Educate on nail hygiene and hand‑washing after toilet use

sections.p: Examiners test understanding of the life cycle, diagnostic nuances, and public‑health control measures.
b: Key clue: nocturnal perianal itching in a child
Scotch‑tape test is the gold‑standard; timing matters
Empirical treatment is acceptable when resources are limited
Re‑treatment after 2 weeks prevents reinfection from eggs laid after the first dose
Differentiating pinworm from other helminths hinges on egg size and lack of systemic symptoms

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of secondary bacterial infection (cellulitis, fever)
Persistent urinary symptoms suggesting urethral involvement

faq.q: Why is the tape test done in the early morning?
faq.a: Female worms lay eggs at night; early‑morning sampling catches the maximum number before washing removes them.
Rarely; the worm burden is low and blood loss is minimal, unlike hookworm.

faq.q: Is a single dose of albendazole enough?
faq.a: One dose kills adult worms, but a second dose 2 weeks later is needed to eradicate larvae that hatch after the first treatment.

exam: A 7‑year‑old presents with night‑time perianal itching; what is your next diagnostic step? — Perform a Scotch‑tape test on three consecutive mornings; if unavailable, start empirical therapy.
Explain why a second dose of albendazole is given 2 weeks after the first. — To eliminate larvae that hatch from eggs laid after the initial dose, breaking the life cycle.

How would you differentiate enterobiasis from trichuriasis in a low‑resource setting? — Pinworm causes nocturnal perianal itching and eggs are detected by tape test; Trichuris causes dysentery‑like symptoms and eggs are seen in stool.

A child from a refugee camp has perianal itching and a low‑grade fever; what complications must you watch for? — Secondary bacterial infection of scratched skin, possible vulvovaginitis or urinary tract infection.

What infection control measures reduce reinfection rates in a school outbreak? — Treat all children and staff, wash bedding in hot water, daily cleaning of toilets with bleach, promote hand‑washing after toileting.
Why is stool microscopy less reliable than the tape test for pinworm? — Eggs are deposited on perianal skin, not consistently shed into stool; thus stool exams miss many infections.

In a HIV‑positive adolescent with chronic pinworm infection, what additional concern is there? — Higher risk of secondary bacterial infection and possible more intense pruritus due to immune dysregulation.
